claims.claim: WVON launched April 1, 1963 on 1450 AM, the former WHFC (1,000-watt, licensed Cicero, IL), purchased by Chess Records owners Leonard and Phil Chess and branded 'Voice of the Negro.'
claims.evidence: Three independent legislative tributes agree on date, frequency, prior call sign, wattage, license city, purchasers, and branding.
claims.notes: Strongest-anchored claim in the brief.
claims.source: Congressional Record Vol. 159 (Rep. Danny K. Davis, 2013); Congressional Record Vol. 165 (Senate tribute via Rep. Bobby Rush, 2019); Illinois HR0201 (98th GA, 2013)
claims.source_type: government record (legislative tribute citing station history)

claims.claim: WVON's launch lineup ('The Good Guys') was Franklin McCarthy, E. Rodney Jones, Herb Kent, Wesley South, and Pervis Spann; later roster included Ric Ricardo, Bill 'Butterball' Crane, Ed Cook, Joe Cobb, Roy Wood, Ed Maloney, Bill 'Doc' Lee, Don Cornelius, Richard Pegue, Isabel Joseph Johnson, Cecil Hale, McKee Fitzhugh; GM Lucky Cordell; 'Ambassador of Good Will' Bernadine C. Washington.
claims.evidence: Identical rosters in two independent legislative sources.
claims.notes: Nicknames for some roster members (e.g., E. Rodney Jones 'Mad Lad') remain unverified — see red-team.

claims.claim: WHFC (pre-1963) aired ethnic and African-American programming through the 1940s–1960s; Ernie Banks hosted a program in the late 1950s; its 97.9 FM sister WEHS simulcast it until adopting a jazz format as WSDM in 1965.
claims.evidence: Trade-press-based station history; corroborated in outline by Jack Cooper's documented 1938 time-buy on WHFC (Ellett 2013).
claims.notes: WHFC-era detail is thinner than WVON-era; FCC History Cards would firm it up.

claims.claim: After Leonard Chess's death in October 1969, the Chess family sold WVON to Globetrotter Communications (George N. Gillett Jr. and Potter Palmer); the sale was consummated in 1970 for a reported $9 million.
claims.evidence: Sale itself verified by HR0201 and Davis 2013 tribute; price and 1970 consummation from station history citing trade press.
claims.notes: Price figure needs a Broadcasting-magazine primary confirmation.
claims.source: Illinois HR0201 (2013); Davis 2013 tribute; WVON station history

claims.claim: On February 5, 1975 at 3:30 p.m., WVON moved from 1450 to the 5,000-watt 1390 AM facility (ex-WNUS), which Globetrotter had bought from the McLendon interests; the 1450 frequency went silent.
claims.evidence: Date, time, wattage, and seller consistent across station histories citing Broadcasting (Mar 10, 1975) and FCC Call Sign History.
claims.notes: 1390 facility history independently verified via WGRB history (FCC Facility ID 51162).
claims.source: WVON/WGRB station histories; Broadcasting via citations

claims.claim: In 1977 Combined Communications Corporation purchased Globetrotter Communications; Combined merged with Gannett Co. in 1978 — the route by which WVON became a Gannett station.
claims.evidence: Consistent across station histories; merger reported in Washington Post (May 9, 1978).
claims.notes: HR0201's shorthand 'sold to Gannett in 1977' compresses this two-step chain.

claims.claim: In 1979 Wesley South and Pervis Spann formed Midway Broadcasting Corporation and, with Migala Communications, took a shared-time arrangement on the silent 1450 frequency: WXOL (Midway, blues) and WCEV ('We're Chicagoland's Ethnic Voice'); both were on the air by October 1979, sharing the 3350 S. Kedzie tower.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Davis 2013 tribute says WXOL 'premiered in August of 1979'; station history says both stations on air 'by October 1979.' Minor month-level discrepancy.
claims.notes: Shared-time arrangement and tower location verified; exact debut month flagged UNRESOLVED.
claims.source: Davis 2013 tribute; WVON station history (citing FCC/shared-time agreement)

claims.claim: WXOL's blues-oriented format sparked an immediate increase in blues record sales in the Chicago area.
claims.evidence: Single station-history claim citing three sources not directly consulted.
claims.notes: Exactly the kind of airplay→sales causal claim this brief needs; requires primary (trade press or label) confirmation.

claims.claim: On October 3, 1983 Gannett changed 1390's call letters from WVON to WGCI; on March 28, 1984 Midway's WXOL took the WVON calls back to 1450, with a reported 50% audience increase after the change.
claims.evidence: Call-sign dates from FCC Call Sign History (via WGRB history); audience claim single-source.
claims.notes: Call changes VERIFIED-equivalent via FCC records; '50% increase' is PROVISIONAL.
claims.source: FCC Call Sign History (via WGRB history); WVON station history

claims.claim: In 1986 WVON (1450 AM, Midway-owned) adopted a Black-oriented talk format — described by HR0201 as Chicago's first Black talk-radio format, done at co-owner Wesley South's urging.
claims.evidence: HR0201 (2013) and Davis 2013 tribute agree on year, owner, and South's role.
claims.notes: 'First' claim is attributed to the legislature, not independently verified against other markets.

claims.claim: On January 16, 1989 the AM station on 1390 (then WGCI, Gannett-owned) debuted an African-American-oriented talk format; it was dropped September 10, 1990 for urban oldies branded 'Dusty Radio.'
claims.evidence: Station history citing Chicago Tribune (James Warren, Sept 11, 1990).
claims.notes: RESOLVES BMI-002 red-team item 24: this 1989 talk debut was on WGCI-AM 1390, a DIFFERENT station from the 1986 WVON-1450 talk flip. The red team conflated them.

claims.claim: WVON served as a civil-rights communications hub: interviews with MLK and Elijah Muhammad; Jesse Jackson called in to report King's assassination; DJs went out with loudspeakers on trucks calling for calm after the 1968 riots.
claims.evidence: Consistent across Davis 2013, Rush/Senate 2019, HR0201; Searcy dissertation (2012) is the scholarly treatment.
claims.notes: Searcy full text not directly consulted; abstract + secondary citations only.

claims.claim: Motown founder Berry Gordy had an arrangement sending every song he produced to WVON before any other station.
claims.evidence: Repeated in HR0201, Davis tribute, and station histories — but all may descend from a single station-lore source.
claims.notes: Classic candidate for myth-as-fact; treat as attributed lore, not established fact.

claims.claim: At its 1960s peak WVON captured 44–48% of Black listeners daily, and three years later 40% of Black households listened weekly (Searcy).
claims.evidence: Cited via DePaul student paper summarizing Searcy pp. 88; dissertation full text not directly consulted.
claims.notes: Ratings figures need Arbitron/primary corroboration before flagship use.

claims.claim: Lu (Lutrelle) Palmer coined the slogan 'We shall see in '83,' hosted 'Lu's Notebook'/'On Target' on WVON-AM 1450 (10 p.m.–midnight), lost sponsors over his politics, and was the single most effective voice in electing Harold Washington mayor in 1983.
claims.evidence: Palmer's own words in the Eyes on the Prize II oral history (1989, AAPB); Chicago Tribune obituary; two Congressional Record tributes.
claims.notes: Corrects BMI-002's anachronism: this was WVON's MUSIC-era political power (1983), not the later talk format.
claims.source: American Archive of Public Broadcasting cpb-aacip-71cf9b5d2fb; Chicago Tribune obituary (via journal-isms); Congressional Record Vol. 147 (2001), Vol. 150 (2004)
claims.source_type: primary (oral history) + reputable journalism + government record

claims.claim: WAAF (950 AM) was sold in 1967 to a corporation formed by Ralph Atlass for $900,000; the call sign became WGRT ('W-Great!') with a soul music format.
claims.evidence: Sale price/buyer from Billboard (Dec 17, 1966, 'Corn Belt Pub. Sells WAAF'); format/call meaning from Pruter's Chicago Soul (1992, scholarly).
claims.notes: FCC History Cards (1927–1980, WAAF/WGRT/WJPC) exist and would firm the exact call-change date.

claims.claim: Daddy-O Daylie continued on WGRT hosting a morning jazz program, cut from two hours to 90 minutes to 30 minutes by 1971.
claims.evidence: Jet (Feb 25, 1971) contemporary report.
claims.notes: Jet is a primary-contemporary Black press source.

claims.claim: On May 29, 1973 Johnson Publishing Company bought 950 AM for $1,800,000; on November 1, 1973 the call sign became WJPC; DJs included Tom Joyner and LaDonna Tittle, with Daddy-O Daylie's Sunday jazz show.
claims.evidence: Purchase price/date from Duncan's American Radio (trade annual) and Ebony (Dec 1973, contemporary Black press); call change from Jet (Nov 15, 1973, contemporary).
claims.notes: Corrects thin BMI-002 record (which had only the HistoryMakers finding aid).

claims.claim: WJPC began nighttime operation (5,000 watts) in 1980; in the late 1980s–early 1990s it simulcast sister 106.3 WLNR's 'Soft Touch' format; at noon July 15, 1992 it flipped to all-rap.
claims.evidence: Station history citing Billboard ('Rap and black radio,' Nov 28, 1992) and M Street Journal (July 8, 1992).
claims.notes: Daytime-only 1967–1980 status is supported by the 1980 nighttime-start fact.
claims.source: Billboard 1992-11-28; M Street Journal 1992-07-08 (via station history)

claims.claim: In 1994 Johnson Publishing sold 950 AM and 106.3 WJPC-FM to Broadcasting Partners for $8 million; the AM became '106 Jamz' WEJM (urban), then sports WIDB (1997), Spanish WNTD (1999), and Relevant Radio Catholic talk (2014).
claims.evidence: Sale prices from NYT (Apr 9, 1997) and Tribune (Apr 9, 1997) via station history; subsequent flips trade-reported.
claims.notes: End of the Black-owned era on 950 AM.

claims.claim: On 1390 AM: Al Benson (born Arthur Leaner) began a Sunday gospel program on WGES in 1945, then hosted a secular blues/jazz/R&B show as 'Al Benson'; later Black DJs included Richard Stamz, Ric Riccardo, Sam Evans, Herb Kent, Franklyn McCarthy, and Sid McCoy.
claims.evidence: Barlow's Voice Over (1999, scholarly, p.98); Pruter's Chicago Soul (1992, p.12); Billboard Apr 13, 1963; Jet Mar 2, 1961.
claims.notes: Benson is the bridge figure between 1940s gospel radio and the DJ era.

claims.claim: On September 1, 1962 the 1390 station was sold to Gordon McLendon for $1M plus $1M non-compete and became WYNR ('Winner') with an all-Black format; the FCC held hearings in 1963 on complaints about dropped foreign-language programming.
claims.evidence: Sale terms from Broadcasting (June 18, 1962); format change from Broadcasting (Sept 3, 1962); FCC hearings from Chicago Tribune (Jan 24, Apr 18, Apr 20, 1963).
claims.notes: Tribune 1963 items are primary-contemporary evidence of radio as contested public sphere.

claims.claim: On September 3, 1964 WYNR became WNUS with an all-news format; in 1965 McLendon bought 107.5 FM (WFMQ) for $400,000, making WNUS-FM a simulcast — described as the first all-news station in the United States.
claims.evidence: Broadcasting (Aug 24, 1964); Billboard (Aug 29, 1964; Dec 5, 1964). 'First all-news' is a standard but attributed claim.
claims.notes: BMI-002 red-team item 16 flagged this as Wikipedia-only; trade citations now located. Keep attributed.

claims.claim: In February 1975 Globetrotter Communications bought 107.5 FM and 1390 AM for $3,550,000; 107.5 became WGCI with a disco format branded 'Studio 107' later that year.
claims.evidence: Broadcasting (Mar 10, 1975, 'CCI heads toward top among groups'); Billboard disco coverage (Nov 1, 1975).
claims.notes: Corrects BMI-002's Wikipedia-only grading.

claims.claim: WGCI shifted from disco to broad urban contemporary in 1980; Tom Joyner simultaneously hosted mornings at KKDA Dallas and afternoons at WGCI ('The Fly Jock'); Doug Banks hosted morning drive 1986–1993.
claims.evidence: Station history citing Billboard and Tribune; Dyson's HistoryMakers finding aid (Dyson hired Banks, gave Steve Harvey his radio break).
claims.notes: Joyner arrangement widely documented; keep as attributed.
claims.source: WGCI-FM history; HistoryMakers Marv Dyson finding aid (2007)

claims.claim: In July 1986 Ralphi Rosario, Kenny Jason, and Mickey Oliver left WBMX's Hot Mix 5 for WGCI-FM's copycat 'Jackmasters'; WGCI cancelled it in February 1987.
claims.evidence: Single fan-archivist source (Mike 'Hitman' Wilson biography, YouTube).
claims.notes: BMI-002 red-team already flagged; unchanged.

claims.claim: WBMX 102.7 FM (Oak Park) took its calls in 1974 ('Black Music EXperience'); it was sold to Sky Broadcasting for $27 million in 1988 and flipped to urban AC 'V103' (WVAZ) on October 18, 1988 at 5 p.m.
claims.evidence: Station histories; sale/flip details trade-reported.
claims.notes: End of the house-music-on-radio era on 102.7.

claims.claim: The Hot Mix 5 was formed in 1981 by WBMX program director Lee Michaels for 'Saturday Night Live, Ain't No Jive' (hosted by Armando Rivera); founding DJs included Farley 'Funkin' Keith, Mickey 'Mixin' Oliver, Ralphi 'Rockin' Rosario, Kenny 'Jammin' Jason, and Scott 'Smokin' Silz.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia + mutually-referential fan archivists; participant account (WBMX.com 'Real Story,' 2006) names Michaels and Rivera but full roster details remain thin.
claims.notes: BMI-002 red-team downgrade stands. City of Chicago Warehouse Landmark Report (2023) VERIFIES the core: WBMX was among the first to broadcast DJs doing live house mixes.
claims.source: Wikipedia; fan archivists; WBMX.com 2006; City of Chicago Warehouse Landmark Report 2023

claims.claim: WBMX's Hot Mix 5 show reached #1 in Chicago ratings with over 2 million listeners.
claims.evidence: Single encyclopedic source; figures uncited there.
claims.notes: Needs Arbitron books — flagged in BMI-002 gaps (item 7). Do not publish the number.

claims.claim: Herb Kent: WBEZ classical program at 16 (1944); WGES (1952); WBEE (1955–60, coined 'dusty records'); WJOB; WHFC; WVON (1962, eight years); 27 years at V103; National Radio Hall of Fame (1995); died Oct 22, 2016, hours after his final broadcast.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Chicago Magazine (2016) says his first professional DJ job was WGRY Gary in 1949 — consistent if WBEZ 1944 counts as student/amateur start.
claims.notes: Career arc consistent across obituaries (Ebony, Final Call, radio-online) and Chicago Magazine; memoir (2009) is the primary source not directly consulted.
claims.source: Ebony 2016; Final Call 2016; radio-online 2016; Chicago Magazine 2016

claims.claim: Pervis Spann: first DJ job at WOPA (Oak Park); organized a B.B. King/Junior Parker concert (1960); hired by Chess as WVON DJ in 1963 ('The Blues Man'); staged an 87-hour sleepless sit-in raising money for MLK.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (Rep. Bobby Rush, Mar 24, 2022); Davis 2013 corroborates Good Guys membership.
claims.notes: The same 2022 tribute's claim that Spann and South 'purchased the station' in 1963 is DISPUTED (below).

claims.claim: Pervis Spann and Wesley South 'purchased the radio station' on April 1, 1963 and created the 'Voice of the Negro' identity.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Contradicted by three legislative sources (Davis 2013, HR0201, Rush/Senate 2019) documenting the Chess purchase; Spann/South's verified station purchase is Midway Broadcasting/WXOL in 1979.
claims.notes: The 2022 Rush tribute is internally inconsistent on this point. Do not publish.
claims.source: Rush 2022 tribute vs. Davis 2013 / HR0201 / Rush-Senate 2019

claims.claim: Yvonne Daniels: announcer on WYNR (early 1960s); hired by WLS in 1973 as its first female air personality (overnights ~8 years); later WVON, WGCI, WNUA; morning host on AM 1390 mid-1980s; died 1991 at 54.
claims.evidence: WYNR role corroborated by Radio Hall of Fame bio; 'first female at WLS' rests on aircheck-archivist biographies.
claims.notes: BMI-002 red-team: needs institutional corroboration.
claims.source: Radio Hall of Fame bio; Ellis Feaster archivist bios; WGRB history

claims.claim: Don Cornelius: hired at WVON in 1966 as announcer/newsreader/DJ; moved to WCIU-TV (1967–68) hosting 'A Black's View of the News'; produced the Soul Train pilot with $400 of his own money (1970); national syndication October 1971.
claims.evidence: Consistent across Black Enterprise, blackamericaweb, TVInsider biographies.
claims.notes: The WVON→Soul Train pipeline is the brief's clearest performer→audience-via-media case.

claims.claim: Jack Cooper debuted 'The All-Negro Hour' on WGBS on November 3, 1929 (ran to 1935); used race records — exempt from the ASCAP ban — because they were cheaper than live talent; bought afternoon time on WSBC and WHFC in 1938; at his 1947 peak sold 40 hours/week across four stations; WAAF's 'Wardrobe Derby' was sponsored by National Credit Clothiers.
claims.evidence: Ellett 2013 (Nostalgia Digest), adapted from Encyclopedia of Black Radio 1921–1955 (McFarland, 2011), citing Cooper biographer Mark Newman.
claims.notes: The ASCAP-exemption→record-economics mechanism is the earliest documented case of the brief's thesis.

claims.claim: Richard Durham wrote 'Democracy–USA' (WBBM, from May 4, 1946), 'Here Comes Tomorrow' (WJJD, Sept 1947 — the first Black soap opera), and 'Destination Freedom' (WMAQ, June 27, 1948–1950); Vernon Jarrett and Oscar Brown Jr. did 'Negro Newsfront' on WJJD (1948–51), one of the first Black radio newscasts in the country.
claims.evidence: Ellett 2013; Durham's Radio Hall of Fame induction (2007) corroborates stature.
claims.notes: Drama/news infrastructure before the DJ era.

claims.claim: Oscar Brown Jr. 'took Negro Newsfront to WVON then WHFC.'
claims.contradictory_evidence: WVON did not exist until 1963; WHFC became WVON. Chronology only works as 'WHFC then WVON' — likely a transposition or memory error in the source chain.
claims.notes: Do not publish as stated; flag for archival verification.

claims.claim: WBEE (Harvey, IL) began in 1955 under Rollins Broadcasting with an R&B format (250 watts daytime, 1,000 watts from 1956); adopted an all-jazz format in 1968.
claims.evidence: Station history with trade citations.
claims.notes: Suburban-licensed Black-appeal station; complements the Chicago-licensed core.

claims.claim: Willie Dixon wrote that in the 1950s 'no disc jockey was going to play your record then without you paying him... They would play 'em two weeks, three times a day and that was it unless you came up with more money.'
claims.evidence: Dixon autobiography, quoted in Donald Clarke's encyclopedia entry on payola.
claims.notes: Primary-voice quote via a reputable secondary; the brief's key evidence for the payola link in the chain.

claims.claim: In 1960 Congress amended the Federal Communications Act to require on-air disclosure of pay-for-play; labels then routed promotion through independent radio promoters as middlemen.
claims.evidence: NPR (McCabe, 2017) with media historian Cynthia Meyers; Univ. of Oregon open textbook chapter.
claims.notes: National context for Chicago's promoter economy.

claims.claim: The FCC's 1978 Statement of Policy on Minority Ownership created the Tax Certificate and Distress Sale programs; minority broadcast ownership rose from ~40 stations (1978) to ~323 (1995, NABOB) or 288 radio + 43 TV (congressional memo); Congress repealed the tax certificate in 1995.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Endpoint figures differ slightly by source (323 vs. 331 total); direction and magnitude agree.
claims.notes: Policy context for Midway (1979) and Johnson Publishing (1973, pre-policy) Black ownership.
claims.source: congress.gov memo 2020; justice.gov SG brief; news.radio-online.com (NABOB)

claims.claim: Under Globetrotter, WVON cut community-service programming to sell more commercials; the public-affairs show 'Hotline' was cut from five to three days a week; the on-air staff was fired in 1977.
claims.evidence: DePaul paper citing Searcy pp. 289–292; Herb Kent quoted on the firings.
claims.notes: Dissertation full text not directly consulted; the commercial-pressure mechanism matters to the brief's advertiser analysis.

claims.claim: Cliff Kelley hosted on WVON for 25 years ('Governor of Talk Radio'); Barack Obama filled in for Kelley in 2002; Roland Martin hosted 2005–2008.
claims.evidence: Rush/Senate 2019 tribute (Kelley); WVON history (Obama, Martin).
claims.notes: Talk-era continuity into the Obama era.

grades.PROVISIONAL: single or thin source; not yet corroborated
grades.SUPPORTED: multiple independent secondary sources, or one strong secondary + primary-adjacent
grades.UNRESOLVED: not yet researched or internally inconsistent
grades.VERIFIED: primary source or ≥2 independent authoritative sources in agreement
